meeting_header:
Date: 2027-05-30
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Evan Pierce (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Laura Mendes (NobleHarbor - Head of Data Governance), Tom Hargreaves (CTO), Aisha Khan (Security Architect), Jon Ruiz (Platform Eng)
Recording: yes
Location: Zoom
summary: Discovery focused on how Redwood can meet NobleHarbor's strict regional residency and keystore requirements. Customer sketched three classes of data (P1: EU-regulated, P2: US-financial, P3: pseudonymized analytics) and emphasized that P1 must never leave EU control plane or have plaintext keys outside EU. Key concerns: KMS residency/escrow, VPC/private deployment feasibility, log redaction and miner-level audit trails, and SLA for fallbacks when dedicated capacity is saturated. Redwood AE/SE walked through hosted/dedicated/private options, keystore routing patterns, and suggested a pilot that validates residency for KMS-bound inference and measures latency with prefix caching enabled.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Logging retention and redaction (EU GDPR & Financial regs)
VPC peering and network egress controls
Fallback routing and model variants for availability
transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today, uh this is Evan from Redwood, joining with Priya our SE. Quick intro?
[00:12] Laura: Hi, I'm Laura Mendes, head of data governance at NobleHarbor. Tom is our CTO, Aisha is security. We're primarily here to figure out if Redwood can meet our residency and keystore requirements.
[00:25] Tom: Yep, big focus is EU personal financial data, GDPR plus our banking regulator. We need to know where keys live and what logs contain.
[00:36] Priya: Totally get it. Can you outline the classes of data you want to keep separated?
[00:42] Laura: Sure. We've got three buckets, P1 is customer financial records that can't leave EU jurisdiction; P2 is US-licensed transaction data that can live in US but needs stronger audit; P3 is anon analytics. The tricky bit is P1 key residency. We need KMS in EU, HSM-backed, and we prefer customer-controlled keys or escrow with onshore custodian.
[01:05] Evan: Understood. Our platform supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. For strict KMS residency the typical pattern is Redwood Private in customer's VPC or a dedicated region with KMS proxies. Priya can explain the keystore routing patterns.
[01:17] Priya: Right, from a runtime perspective we do keystore routing at the control-plane handshake. For Private you own the keystore, Redwood's inference nodes can be deployed in your VPC or in a private tenancy we provision in the EU region. For Dedicated we can pair regional keystores and use envelope encryption so plaintext never leaves the HSM.
[01:36] Aisha: A couple follow ups: do you support HSMs like AWS CloudHSM or on-prem Thales? Also, can you escrow keys with a third party?
[01:45] Priya: We have documented integrations with AWS KMS/CloudHSM and we support customer-managed HSMs in Private deployments. Escrow is possible but it's a legal and ops process — we can provide guidance and references. I'll flag that as a next step for legal.
[01:58] Tom: How about logs? Even if keys are in EU, logs often contain model inputs, sometimes PII. We need guaranteed redaction and an auditable chain.
[02:08] Evan: Good point. Our console can filter and redact tokens at ingestion, and for Private you can configure log retention policies and disable model input persistence entirely. We also offer per-tenant audit logs with immutable event streams.
[02:21] Laura: When you say redact at ingestion, is that deterministic? We need to know if anything could leak before redaction.
[02:29] Priya: There's a short window during the ingestion pipeline; on Private deployments that window is within your VPC and can be minimized. We also have an optional local pre-filter you can run inside your environment to strip fields before sending to the runtime.
[02:41] Jon: For network controls, will Redwood accept VPC peering and static egress IPs so our firewall rules can be strict?
[02:48] Priya: Yes, VPC peering is supported for Private, and for Dedicated we provide allowlistable egress addresses; some customers put a NAT in front and route traffic.
[02:56] Tom: Performance-wise we've got tight latency SLOs: 100ms p95 for short prompts, but for longer multi-turn sessions we tolerate higher. Can you hit that with envelope encryption and KMS in EU?
[03:09] Evan: It's a tradeoff. KMS calls add milliseconds; envelope encryption minimizes KMS roundtrips, but if the HSM is cross-region it will add latency. For EU-only HSMs in-region, the hit is small. SE will propose a pilot with prefix caching and batching to show numbers.
[03:25] Laura: Also need to know what happens when dedicated capacity is saturated — the regulator expects graceful degradation not silent failure.
[03:33] Priya: We support fallback policies: route to a compatible model variant in a neighboring region or degrade features (e.g., reduced context length) while signaling via telemetry. For P1 data we can block fallback out of region unless you allow it.
[03:47] Aisha: If fallback is blocked, what's the outage SLA? Do you have runbooks for legal holds and evidence export?
[03:53] Evan: We have documented runbooks. For Private, the operator controls fallback. We can commit to notification SLAs and provide exportable encrypted evidence bundles. We'll include that in the SOC2 supplemental.
[04:07] Tom: Can you do canary deploys and A/B routing while keeping data partitioned by tenant? We want to run a canary on a new quantized model but not risk P1 exposure.
[04:17] Priya: Yes. Rollouts are per-tenant and per-route. You can target subsets of traffic and pin P1 tenants to a stable execution path. Canary traffic can be run on P3 or internal test tenants first.
[04:29] Laura: We have a compliance requirement to keep logs for seven years for some financial instruments. Is that supported and where would logs be stored?
[04:37] Evan: Retention is configurable. For Private, you'd retain logs in your object store; for Dedicated we can support long-term retention in region-locked buckets with access controls and retention locking. We'll surface retention policies in the proposal.
[04:50] Jon: One operational concern: our platform uses a service mesh and mTLS. Can Redwood fit into that architecture?
[04:56] Priya: You can deploy the inference agents behind your mesh, and our control-plane connectors speak mTLS. We'll need the cert rotation cadence to align.
[05:05] Tom: About evidence for audits — does Redwood provide signable audit events? We need tamper-evident logs.
[05:12] Evan: Yes, we emit signed audit events and we can provide hash-chained logs for Private deployments. For Dedicated we offer signing via our control plane with exportable verification keys.
[05:23] Laura: Are there any compliance gaps you've seen with banks that we should preempt?
[05:28] Priya: Common gaps: key residency misunderstandings, inadvertent cross-region failover, and lack of PI redaction before logs land in third-party analytics. We'll propose guardrails: explicit allowed fallbacks, pre-filtering, and keystore residency verification as part of the pilot.
[05:42] Aisha: On legal — we'll need an answer about escrow. We have an internal risk team that prefers a custodian escrow model.
[05:48] Evan: We can introduce you to partners that handle escrow; it's usually a separate contract. We'll include typical vendor references in the package.
[05:57] Tom: Ok let's walk through a potential pilot — scope and metrics.
[06:02] Priya: Pilot suggestion: 4-week pilot, two tenants (one P1 EU, one P3 test), deploy Redwood Private nodes in EU region, use customer KMS, validate end-to-end that no plaintext leaves EU, run latency benchmarks with prefix caching on 4k token sequences, verify log redaction and audit exports. Metrics: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, percent of requests hitting prefix cache, and number of KMS roundtrips.
[06:33] Laura: That sounds reasonable. Cost is a factor; if Private is expensive, can Dedicated with strict keystore binding be an intermediary?
[06:40] Evan: Yes, Dedicated with region-locked keystore is often a middle ground. It provides predictable capacity and cost savings versus fully private on-prem. We can model costs for both.
[06:50] Jon: For the telemetry side, will you expose per-token cost and a breakdown so we can map to our chargeback model?
[06:57] Priya: Yes, per-token and per-route cost breakdown is available via the console and API. We can create a sample report for finance.
[07:06] Aisha: About SSO/SAML and RBAC — we need integration into our identity provider and fine-grained role separation for operators vs auditors.
[07:14] Evan: We support SAML, OIDC, SCIM provisioning, and role-based policies. For Private we let you map roles to your internal groups.
[07:23] Laura: Any gotchas with GDPR Data Subject Requests when using Redwood?
[07:28] Priya: For Hosted customers, data subject request handling needs coordination; for Private, you own the storage and can execute deletion. We'll document required API calls and timelines.
[07:39] Tom: One more technical nit: you mentioned prefix/KV caching. How do you guarantee cache privacy across tenants?
[07:46] Priya: Caches are tenant-scoped; we shard the KV cache per tenant and optionally per-tenant key derivation to prevent cross-tenant leakage. There's also an in-memory TTL and eviction policy you can tune.
[07:58] Laura: For the KMS pattern, is envelope encryption mandatory or optional? We prefer envelope so KMS hits are minimized.
[08:04] Priya: Envelope is recommended and is the default for production workloads. That keeps KMS calls to the key-wrapping/unwrapping lifecycle rather than per-request plaintext ops.
[08:12] Evan: A note about fallback again — if you block cross-region fallback for P1, you could face availability windows; we can put in automatic notification and escalation and recommend a DR runbook.
[08:24] Aisha: We'll ask our ops team to run failure-mode testing.
[08:28] Evan: Great. We'll also surface an ops checklist.
[08:31] Tom: Ok can we talk about metrics you'll collect for the pilot and what we have to give you?
[08:36] Priya: We'll collect latency distributions, KMS call rates, cache hit ratios, token throughput, and telemetry for any fallback decisions. We'll need a sample traffic profile and a few anonymized prompt templates from you.
[08:50] Laura: We can share templates stripped of PII. For P1 we can't send real customer rows, but we can provide synthetic equivalents that preserve shape.
[08:58] Evan: That works. We'll show how we run the prefix-cache benchmark in the pilot.
[09:03] Jon: One more ops question — can we export audit logs to our SIEM?
[09:07] Priya: Yes, we support exports to common sinks (S3, Splunk, Datadog) and push via secure connectors. For Private you control that pipeline.
[09:16] Laura: On contract items: we need indemnities for regulated-data breaches and clarity on notification timelines.
[09:22] Evan: We'll have legal follow up. Typical timelines are 24-72 hours for incident notification; we can discuss exact SLAs in the enterprise attachment.
[09:33] Aisha: Regarding encryption in transit — we require mTLS everywhere and FIPS-validated crypto for certain flows. Do you support FIPS stacks?
[09:42] Priya: FIPS crypto is supported for Dedicated and Private. We'll need to document which components run FIPS modules and any performance implications.
[09:52] Tom: Competitors question — we've spoken to other vendors with hosted offerings. Why would Redwood be better for us?
[09:58] Evan: Two reasons: production-first controls and consistent runtime across hosting modes. We don't force you to re-architect when you move from Hosted to Private. Also our billing/telemetry and fine-grained routing give you predictable economics when you scale.
[10:13] Laura: Ok, let's recap the agreed next steps.
[10:17] Evan: Redwood: SOC2+ supplemented docs, KMS integration spec, pilot SLO proposal, sample cost model for Dedicated vs Private.
[10:25] Laura: NobleHarbor: provide data-flow diagram, anonymized prompt set, ops contact for VPC/peering.
[10:31] Tom: We'll coordinate legal intro for escrow discussion.
[10:36] Evan: Great. Priya will run the benchmark and Evan will follow up with the docs.
[10:41] Priya: One small note — sometimes the transcription shows KV cache as K V cash in our runbooks, ignore that.
[10:48] Laura: (laugh) Noted.
[10:51] Evan: Thanks everyone, we'll aim to get materials out within the week.
[10:55] Aisha: Thanks all.
[10:57] [END OF RECORDING]

Note: Transcript includes a few mis-attributed lines and minor recognition errors; names and acronyms may be slightly garbled in places (common with automated transcription).
